newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Sears poised for major shake-up.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Sears poised for major shake-up.

text.p: The break-up or shake-up of Sears Plc looks to be on the cards when the British retailing conglomerate reports annual results next Tuesday.

The group's embattled chief executive Liam Strong was expected to put restructuring plans to the board on Thursday, including rationalisation of loss-making British Shoe Corporation, retail analysts said.
They said this was Strong's last chance to try and restore value to Sears' shares, which were languishing near historic lows at around 78-1/2 pence at the close on Thursday.
"The logic goes that he will go unless he can demonstrate some way of adding value to the whole thing," said one retail analyst, who asked not to be identified.

Strong, hired in 1992 to streamline Sears' hotch-potch of retail businesses, has become increasingly accident-prone in his attempts to put some spark back into the company, which has performed poorly despite an upbeat retail economy.
Institutional investors are said to be losing patience and now pressing for a management change.
"He's up against a wall, this is his last chance," said another retail analyst.

Strong's latest misfortune was being outmanoeuvred in efforts to sell Sears' Freemans mail order arm. Littlewoods is currently negotiating to buy the business, but analysts expect a substantially lower price the original 395 million stg after rival bidder N.Brown Group Plc pulled out.
Strong has promised to return proceeds from the sale to shareholders, but this could be delayed as the deal with Littlewoods had been referred to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission.
Analysts' believed drastic action such as demerging Sears' profitable Selfridges department store was long overdue, but were uncertain whether the restructuring would go this far.
Sears' shares were being weighed down by the negative value ascribed to British Shoe Corporation and the price might recover if BSC was ditched, analysts said.
But they said BSC needed radical pruning and that moves to close Shoe Express or sell Dolcis shoe stores would not be enough.
"The key issue is what he does with British Shoe," said Nick Bubb at MeesPierson, who suggested Sears might end up destroying value by simply writing off more stores.
Strong has already performed major surgery on BSC and introduced new formats, including Shoe Express, a self-service, low-price shoe store, but this had not worked, analysts said.
"They lack exposure to sportswear and branded footwear, which have been the more buoyant parts of the market," said another retail analyst.

The group, which also owns womens fashion chains such as Wallis and Warehouse, is forecast to make pretax profits for the year to end January 1997 of between 75 million to 80 million stg, down from 100 million last time.

Analysts say Sears' Freemans' home shopping arm, which is up for sale, is likely to have suffered from uncertainty about its future, British Shoe Corporation will have traded poorly and Selfridges, usually the star profit performer, will be hit by the strong pound.
Forecasts for the current year (1997/98) look vulnerable because of the group's poor returns. "Profit, cash flow and dividend projections all remain at risk," said another retail analyst.
British press reports have suggested Sears would reshape the group into two divisions, Selfridges and womenswear, and would be able to shed BSC at a cost of 50 million stg.
There has been persistent speculation about a break-up of the entire group, including a spin off of Selfridges, valued at some 550 million stg.
--Jane Merriman, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
